item.title: LORE: An open-source AI reader that builds knowledge graphs from e-books with citation support
item.description:
LORE: An open-source AI reader that builds knowledge graphs from e-books with citation support

LORE is an open-source AI reader that transforms e-books into interactive knowledge graphs, answering questions with every sentence cited and respecting the user’s reading progress without revealing later spoilers.

📚 What LORE Does

LORE turns each book into a knowledge graph of its characters, places, groups and events, then answers questions from the text itself. Every sentence in an answer cites the passage it comes from, and a second pass checks each citation against that passage and removes anything the book doesn’t say.

🔍 How It Tracks Progress

Users can set their reading progress per book, and all outputs—answers, the graph, character profiles, and timelines—stop at the specified chapter. This is enforced at retrieval, ensuring the model never sees what comes later in the book.

🧩 Key Features

  • Answers questions about characters, places, and events
  • Provides character profiles, story timelines, and relationship maps
  • Supports long, sectioned analyses with full citations
  • Click any character for detailed profiles with passage-backed information
  • Handles tracking character changes across multiple books
  • Manages complex world and magic system explanations

⚙️ Technical Implementation

LORE uses Gemini (free tier works), Claude, or OpenAI for reading and writing; embeddings run locally on Ollama. An MCP server enables integration with Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and other MCP clients to search libraries and ask questions.

Users can choose their AI model on the admin page, with options including self-hosted models like llama.cpp’s llama-server, vLLM, LM Studio, or Ollama. Each person added to the system gets their own private library.

🚀 Availability and Setup

Self-hosting requires Python 3.12+, uv, Node.js 18+, and Ollama. The local embedding model is installed via ollama pull nomic-embed-text. A Gemini API key (or Claude/OpenAI key) is required, which can be stored in an environment variable or in ~/.config/lore/gemini.env.

The fastest option is the hosted beta at lore.jrvn.site, where new accounts start with A Study in Scarlet already processed for immediate use. Setup involves opening the app, adding books via EPUB or PDF, and waiting for processing to complete.

💡 Integration Options

LORE runs an MCP server, allowing Claude to search the library and ask questions with reading position constraints. The hosted beta integrates at claude.ai via Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector using https://lore.jrvn.site/mcp. Self-hosted instances run through uv run lore mcp (stdio) or uv run lore mcp --http.

item.title: MCPM v2.0 releases a global configuration model for MCP servers

MCPM v2.0 releases a global configuration model for MCP servers

MCPM v2.0 has been released as an open source CLI tool for managing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. 🔍 Overview

The tool is designed to be AI Agent Friendly, offering a non-interactive CLI with comprehensive automation support and an llm.txt guide.

🧩 How it works

The v2.0 architecture uses a global configuration model where servers are installed once and organized with virtual profiles. These profiles act as tags to organize servers into logical groups for different workflows. Once organized, servers can be integrated into specific MCP clients as needed.

⚙️ Key details

Key features of MCPM v2.0 include:

  • Global Server Management: Install servers once, use everywhere
  • Virtual Profiles: Organize servers with tags for different workflows
  • Server Discovery: Browse and install from the MCP Registry
  • Direct Execution: Run servers over stdio or HTTP for testing
  • Public Sharing: Share servers through secure tunnels

item.title: Octocode: A Rust CLI and MCP server for codebase intelligence
item.description:
Octocode: A Rust CLI and MCP server for codebase intelligence

Octocode is a Rust CLI and MCP server designed for exploring codebases by combining semantic search, structural search, and a live graph of symbols and dependencies. It provides AI agents, such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Windsurf, with deep understanding of code structures through a single binary.

🧩 How it works

The tool integrates several capabilities to assist with code exploration:

  • Find code by intent: Uses hybrid vector and keyword search with configurable reranking.
  • Locate definitions and usages: Performs structural search over the current source.
  • Trace relationships: Maps imports, calls, inheritance, and implementations between files and symbols.
  • Read signatures: Accesses function signatures without loading entire files, optionally using a language server for definitions, references, and hover information.
  • Run locally: Utilizes default embedding and reranking models or configurable remote providers.

⚙️ Key details

Octocode operates through specific tools that differ in their indexing requirements:

Tool Use it for Requires an index
semantic_search Find code, documentation, and indexed history by meaning Yes
structural_search Find definitions, usages, and AST patterns in current source No
view_signatures Read function signatures, declarations, and imports No
graphrag Explore live file and symbol relationships and dependency paths No
lsp_* Definitions, references, hover information, symbols, and completion No; requires a language server

Structural search, signatures, and the live dependency graph read the current source directly and function without an index. In contrast, semantic search relies on an index created by running commands in the project’s Git repository. The default configuration uses local FastEmbed models, which download on first use without requiring an API key. For directories without Git, users can apply octocode index --no-git.

🚀 Availability

Installation methods include:

  • Using an installer on Linux or macOS, or in a Unix-compatible shell on Windows.
  • Downloading a binary from GitHub Releases or installing the published crate.
  • Building from source, which requires Rust 1.95 or later and protoc.

Users can integrate Octocode with various MCP clients by installing it where the client can find it on the PATH and adding an entry to the client’s MCP configuration. Additionally, the companion AI agent runtime, Octomind, includes Octocode and OctoFS capabilities in its developer:general agent. The first run of Octomind may install required tools and ask for model credentials.

item.title: Obsidian Gains Local REST API with MCP Server for Secure Vault Access
item.description:
Obsidian Gains Local REST API with MCP Server for Secure Vault Access

A new plugin provides a secure REST API and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Obsidian vaults, enabling scripts, browser extensions, and AI agents to interact directly with vault contents.

🔍 Overview

The plugin exposes a secure, authenticated REST API alongside an MCP server, both serving the same core capabilities. All requests are served over HTTPS with a locally generated certificate and gated behind API key authentication.

🧩 How it works

The MCP server runs at https://127.0.0.1:27124/mcp/ and requires a bearer token in the Authorization header. A plain HTTP endpoint is also available at http://127.0.0.1:27123/mcp/ if enabled.

⚙️ Key details

  • Authentication: HTTPS with locally generated certificate, API key authentication, bearer token for MCP clients
  • Certificate: CA is name-constrained to localhost, 127.0.0.1, and configured hostnames; HTTP endpoint available for easier setup
  • Download CA: Certificate authority available at https://127.0.0.1:27134/obsidian-local-rest-api.crt
  • Vault operations: Full CRUD on any file including binary files, surgically patch specific sections (headings, blocks, frontmatter), search with full-text or JsonLogic queries, follow vault events via Server-Sent Events
  • Active file: Read or write the currently open note in Obsidian
  • Commands: List and execute any Obsidian command, query tags with usage counts, open specific files in UI
  • Extensibility: Other plugins can register their own routes via an API extension interface

🚀 Availability

After installing and enabling the plugin, users can find their API key and certificate in Settings → Local REST API.

item.title: AnythingMCP Launched as an Open-Source Gateway for AI Model Connectivity
item.description:
AnythingMCP Launched as an Open-Source Gateway for AI Model Connectivity

AnythingMCP is a newly released open-source, self-hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway designed to connect AI clients like Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini to enterprise software and internal documents without the need for developers to write custom MCP servers.

🧩 Core Architecture and Features

AnythingMCP functions as a central layer that stores enterprise data in a unified “knowledge graph of how your systems connect,” alongside AI skills and company memory. This data is shared across all connected AI clients while respecting individual user roles.

Key Technical Capabilities

  • Extensive Connectivity: Offers 957 ready connectors supporting over 12,000 tools, including integrations with SAP, Odoo, weclapp, and Amazon Seller. 51 of these connectors operate without an API key.
  • Custom Protocol Support: Provides 696 catalog connectors or supports custom REST, OpenAPI, SOAP, GraphQL, OData, SQL, IMAP, SMTP, and MCP sources. Tools register at runtime.
  • Document Indexing: Indexes SFTP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV (Nextcloud, NAS), S3, and network shares. It extracts data from PDF pages, Excel rows (including column names), Word documents, PowerPoint files, and Outlook emails with attachments.
  • Traceability: AI answers are returned with specific file, page, and date references for verification.
  • File Management: Generates temporary download links for user files and AI-generated files (such as CSV exports or reports), supporting both internal and public access with expiration and revocation capabilities.
  • Cross-Client Memory: Facts and preferences saved in one AI client are accessible in others (e.g., data entered in Claude is usable by Copilot). Memory is managed with personal and company scopes, organized by folders and role limits.
  • Agent Procedures: Supports procedures that AI agents follow, which can be written manually or learned from actual requests.

⚙️ Usage Example

The gateway enables complex queries spanning multiple systems, such as asking a single question in Claude that is answered using data from Etsy, SAP, and a logistics API simultaneously.

🚀 Availability and Usage

  • Cloud Presence: AnythingMCP Cloud hosts over 16,000 workspaces and processes more than 1.5 million AI tool calls per month.
  • Listing Status: The service is listed in the official Claude directory and the ChatGPT Plugin Directory.
  • Trial Access: A free 7-day trial of the Cloud service is available.

item.title: DeepFabric generates synthetic data for language model training
item.description:
DeepFabric generates synthetic data for language model training

DeepFabric is a tool designed to generate synthetic training data for language models and agent evaluations. It combines reasoning traces with tool-calling patterns to create high-quality, domain-specific datasets that teach models to think, plan, and act effectively, call tools correctly, and conform to strict schema structures.

🔍 Overview

The system distinguishes itself through unique topic graph generation algorithms that ensure high diversity while maintaining domain-anchored relevance. This approach guides sample creation to cover all necessary subtopics while avoiding redundancy, a common issue in other tools that can lead to model overfitting.

🧩 How it works

  • Data Generation: The process involves constrained decoding and response validation.
  • Tool Execution: Real tool executions occur within isolated webassembly environments.
  • Accuracy: These mechanisms ensure generated samples strictly adhere to structured schemas, variable constraints, and execution correctness, providing exact syntax and structure for training pipelines.
  • Tool Definitions: Tool definitions can be imported directly from MCP (Model Context Protocol) server schemas, automatically mocked, or based on real-life interfaces.
  • Standard Tools: A standard set of common tools, such as list_files() and read_file(), is included.

⚙️ Key details

  • Deployment Options: DeepFabric can be used as a library, a CLI tool, or via YAML configuration.
  • Configuration: The YAML configuration includes three main sections and optional shared LLM defaults.
  • Mocked Execution: Using mocked tool execution requires a running Spin service, which is provided in a Docker image.
  • Example Output: A specific configuration generated a topic graph with 27 unique nodes, resulting in 27 training samples saved to dataset.jsonl and achieving 100% topic coverage.

🚀 Availability

  • Integration: Generated datasets can be automatically uploaded to Hugging Face.
  • Training Frameworks: Data can be directly imported into popular training frameworks, including TRL, Unsloth, and Axolotl.
  • Evaluation: A built-in evaluation engine assesses model performance on unseen tasks derived from training splits, covering evaluation-only questions, answers, and tool traces.

item.title: ToolHive: An enterprise platform for managing Model Context Protocol servers
item.description:
ToolHive: An enterprise platform for managing Model Context Protocol servers

ToolHive is an enterprise-grade platform designed for running and managing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. It allows organizations to run any MCP server securely, instantly, and anywhere, addressing the need for secure and observable MCP infrastructure in production environments.

🔍 Overview

ToolHive addresses the challenges of managing MCP servers by providing a modular architecture that streamlines secure server management and integration. Unlike most MCP solutions that are SaaS-based, ToolHive allows companies to self-host their MCP registry and gateway, which is particularly useful when compliance requirements prohibit sensitive information from being processed by SaaS providers. The platform includes a Kubernetes operator, enabling teams to declare policies and integrate with identity and observability stacks using familiar tools and patterns.

🧩 How it works

At its core, ToolHive wraps every MCP server in an isolated container with a minimal permission file that does not include local credentials. This isolation helps enforce security standards. The platform uses semantic tool search to reduce token usage by up to 85%. When configured with an authentication source, ToolHive enforces identity and access policy per request, giving platform teams the observability required for production environments. It also provides audit logs and configurable identity enforcement to address security concerns regarding shadow MCP use by developers.

⚙️ Key details

The platform offers a range of features for managing MCP infrastructure, including:

  • Defining dedicated endpoints for secure and efficient team access to tools
  • Orchestrating multiple tools into a virtual MCP using a deterministic workflow engine
  • Centralizing control of security policy, authentication, authorization, and auditing
  • Integrating with Identity Providers (IdP) for Single Sign-On (SSO) via OIDC/OAuth compatibility
  • Customizing and filtering tools and descriptions to improve performance and reduce token usage
  • Connecting with local clients such as Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and VS Code Server
  • Curating a catalog of trusted servers for quick discovery and deployment
  • Integrating with the official MCP registry and adding custom MCP servers
  • Grouping servers based on role or use case
  • Managing the registry via an API-driven interface or embedding it in existing workflows
  • Verifying provenance and signing servers with built-in security controls
  • Providing preset configurations and permissions for a frictionless user experience

🚀 Availability

ToolHive supports flexible deployment options to suit different organizational needs. Users can deploy MCP servers in the cloud via Kubernetes for enterprise scalability, or run them locally via Docker or Podman. Additionally, the platform can proxy remote MCP servers securely for unified management. Organizations can pilot the entire platform and, when ready to scale, leverage Stacklok’s added capabilities and expert team support.

item.title: x64dbg-MCP Server enables AI control of debuggers via Zig
item.description:
x64dbg-MCP Server enables AI control of debuggers via Zig

The x64dbg-MCP Server, a native MCP (Model Context Protocol) plugin for x64dbg, has been released, allowing MCP-compatible AI assistants to control the debugger programmatically over HTTP. Built with the Zig programming language, the solution is designed to be dependency-free, requiring only a single binary drop-in deployment without the need for .NET, Python, or other runtimes.

🧩 How it works

The server exposes the full functionality of x64dbg through standard protocols, enabling AI agents to perform complex debugging tasks. It supports both Streamable HTTP and SSE (Server-Sent Events) transports using JSON-RPC 2.0, ensuring compatibility with both new and legacy MCP clients.

  • Transport Protocols: Uses Streamable HTTP + SSE for dual-transport compatibility.
  • Authentication: Implements mandatory Bearer token authentication; the token is auto-generated on the first run and required for every request to prevent unauthorized access.
  • Execution: The plugin is a pure native application with zero dependencies, cross-compiling to both x32 and x64 architectures from a single codebase.

⚙️ Key details

The MCP server provides extensive control over the debugging environment, covering a wide range of operations from code analysis to memory management.

  • MCP Tools: The evidence cites 84 MCP tools for full debugger control, including disassembly, stepping, breakpoints, memory allocation, registers, modules, threads, call stack, pattern scanning, string extraction, xrefs, symbols, bookmarks, PE analysis, OEP detection, module dumping, PEB/SEH inspection, and tracing. (Note: One quote also references 72 MCP tools covering the workflow).
  • Event Callbacks: Includes 22 event callbacks covering init, stop, breakpoint, exception, step, attach/detach, DLL load/unload, and thread events.
  • Configuration: Users can change IP, port, and token settings via a dialog in the Plugins menu, which auto-restarts the server upon saving.
  • Auto-Start: The MCP server initiates automatically when x64dbg launches.
Component Details
Default Port (x64) 0.0.0.0:9094
Default Port (x32) 0.0.0.0:9095
Language Zig
Dependencies None (No .NET, Python, or runtimes)
Architectures x32 and x64

🚀 Availability

Deployment is designed to be straightforward, allowing users to build and deploy the plugin across different operating systems.

  1. Copy the contents of the dist/ directory into the x64dbg root folder to deploy both x32 and x64 versions.
  2. Launch x64dbg; the MCP server starts automatically.
  3. For connections from WSL or remote machines, set the bind address to 0.0.0.0 in the config dialog and use the host’s IP address.

The tool supports cross-compiling Windows plugins from Linux, macOS, or WSL environments from a single command.

item.title: MiniRAG v2 Alpha Brings Local-First Hybrid Search to MCP Clients
item.description:
MiniRAG v2 Alpha Brings Local-First Hybrid Search to MCP Clients

MiniRAG v2 is now available as a test pre-release (2.0.0aN), offering a local-first Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Model Context Protocol (MCP) server written in Python. The update introduces hybrid search capabilities over local documents, allowing MCP clients to access semantic and keyword-based retrieval without external network dependencies for indexing or querying.

🧩 How it works

The system uses a Python, MCP-native approach built on fastmcp, fastembed, and LanceDB. It performs hybrid search by fusing vector similarity with keyword ranking via weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion, ensuring exact identifiers and error codes surface alongside semantically similar passages. An optional cross-encoder can rerank the best results. The server ships a routing policy that directs questions answerable by documents to the index rather than relying on the model’s memory.

  • Ingestion: 12 file formats are ingested via markitdown, including PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML, CSV, EPUB, Jupyter notebooks, Markdown, and plain text. Standalone images and image-only PDFs are processed locally using Tesseract and Apple Vision on macOS.
  • Search Scope: Keyword search covers both document titles and body text. An informative filename serves as the title if the document’s own heading is boilerplate. Struck-through text remains searchable but is marked to prevent citation as current.
  • Privacy: Nothing leaves the machine during local file ingestion, indexing, or querying. Only one-time model downloads and explicit ingest_url calls for web pages touch the network. The embedding, reranker, and labelling models can optionally run in a separate llama.cpp server.

⚙️ Key details

The release includes 11 MCP tools and a CLI for managing indexes without an MCP client. The server can host multiple indexes defined in indexes.toml over local HTTP, secured by a token. The default embedding model, intfloat/multilingual-e5-large, supports approximately 100 languages. Results are returned in small units (transcript windows, headings, slides, or tables) that fit the model’s 250-token window, reducing cost. The tool also identifies documents that share significant text with query results, indicating potential versions or template siblings.

🚀 Availability

The minirag-mcp package version 2.0.0aN is a test pre-release. Installation commands like pip install minirag-mcp currently install version 1.1.1, which is documented in its specific README.

Activepieces Updates Open Source AI Automation and MCP Toolkit

Activepieces has introduced an all-in-one AI automation platform featuring an extensible, type-safe pieces framework written in TypeScript. The platform offers over 280 open-source pieces available on npmjs.com, with 60% contributed by the community. When contributed, these pieces automatically become available as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for use with LLMs through Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Windsurf.

  • Human Input Interfaces: Built-in support for chat and form interface triggers.

item.title: Hayhooks deploys AI agents and pipelines as REST and MCP endpoints
item.description:
Hayhooks deploys AI agents and pipelines as REST and MCP endpoints

Hayhooks allows developers to deploy Python wrappers or YAML pipelines as typed, validated endpoints, supporting REST APIs, OpenAI-compatible chat, MCP tools, and A2A agents with durable execution and built-in tracing.

🧩 How it works

  • Endpoint Generation: Deployments use method type hints to validate requests and generate the API schema.
  • Protocol Support: The system supports REST APIs, OpenAI-compatible chat completions, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, and Agent2Agent (A2A) agents.
  • UI Integration: Users can connect Open WebUI or use the embedded Chainlit UI to chat with agents.

⚙️ Key details

  • Streaming & Responses: Serves streaming Chat Completions and Responses endpoints, with responses arriving as server-sent events.
  • Durable Execution: Long-running work is checkpointed in Redis, allowing the system to wait for human approval, retry failures, and recover after restarts.
  • Observability: Executions and component traces can be inspected in a terminal dashboard or exported to an OpenTelemetry backend using hayhooks[tracing].
  • MCP & A2A Capabilities: Runs an MCP server that exposes pipelines and agents as tools for Cursor, Claude Desktop, and other clients. Exposes chat-capable pipelines through the Agent2Agent protocol with generated agent cards for discovery and task delegation.

🚀 Availability

  • Requirements: Python 3.10 through 3.14 and an OpenAI API key are required.
  • Access: API docs are available at http://localhost:1416/docs for inspection and testing.

item.title: Kong Gateway introduces AI traffic capabilities and MCP governance
item.description:
Kong Gateway introduces AI traffic capabilities and MCP governance

Kong or Kong Gateway is a cloud-native, platform-agnostic, scalable API, LLM, and MCP Gateway distinguished for its high performance and extensibility via plugins. It provides advanced AI traffic capabilities with multi-LLM support, semantic security, MCP traffic security and analytics, and more.

🔍 Overview

Kong serves as the central layer for orchestrating microservices or conventional API traffic - and agentic LLM and MCP as well - with ease. By providing functionality for proxying, routing, load balancing, health checking, and authentication, it manages traffic across various architectures.

⚙️ Key details

  • Universal LLM API: Routes traffic across multiple providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, GCP Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure AI, Databricks, Mistral, and Huggingface.
  • MCP Capabilities: Includes MCP traffic governance, security, observability, and autogeneration from any RESTful API.
  • AI Features: Offers over 60 features such as AI observability, semantic security, caching, and semantic routing.
  • Security and Routing: Supports authentication and authorization via JWT, basic auth, OAuth, and ACLs.
  • Traffic Management: Handles proxying, SSL/TLS termination, and connectivity support for L4 or L7 traffic.
  • Plugins: Includes 60+ plugins for traffic controls, rate limiting, request/response transformations, logging, and monitoring.
Feature Description
Advanced Routing Load balancing and health checking configurable via RESTful admin API or declarative configuration
Deployment Models Supports Declarative Databaseless Deployment and Hybrid Deployment with control plane/data plane separation
Kubernetes Support Runs natively on Kubernetes thanks to its official Kubernetes Ingress Controller
Plugin Hub Showcases Kong Inc. and community-developed plugins like AWS Lambda, Correlation ID, and Response Transformer

🚀 Availability

Kong is available in various distributions depending on the deployment environment. Users can run it in the cloud, on bare metal, or using containers.

  • Cloud: Sign up for a free trial of Kong Konnect to get started with a cloud-hosted solution.
  • Docker: The docker-compose distribution is suggested for easy setup. A docker installation procedure is also available for running the Kong Gateway in DB-less mode.
  • Installation: To start with the Docker distribution, clone the Docker repository and navigate to the compose folder. Use the command $ KONG_DATABASE=postgres docker-compose --profile database up to start the Gateway stack.

Once started, the Gateway is available on localhost with the following ports:

  • 8000: Send traffic to your service via Kong.
  • 8001: Configure Kong using Admin API or via decK.
  • 8002: Access Kong’s management Web UI (Kong Manager).

item.title: Linear pivots to agent orchestration as AI creates over half of its issues
item.description:
Linear pivots to agent orchestration as AI creates over half of its issues

Linear, an issue tracker founded to replace legacy tools, has pivoted toward becoming a product development system built around agent orchestration. This shift coincided with CEO Karri Saarinen publishing a post titled “Issue tracking is dead,” a sentiment with which most of the company’s customers agreed. Today, more than half of the issues created in Linear originate from AI agents, marking a significant change in how the product is used.

🧩 The Shift to Agent Orchestration

When Cristina joined Linear in 2023, the company had about 40 people and one salesperson. Three weeks after joining, she crossed “move upmarket to enterprise” off the company goals. Instead of chasing enterprise deals, Linear focused on its core user base and later built infrastructure to support autonomous agents.

  • MCP Server: Linear shipped its Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in May 2025, which Cristina says was basically the first in its category.
  • Agent Platform: The company built a platform for building agents into Linear, accompanied by a new set of APIs.
  • Integrations: Linear launched integrations with Codex, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.
  • Linear Agent: The company released its own specific agent solution.

These developments were not part of a pre-planned enterprise roadmap; instead, agents happened, and Linear built the necessary infrastructure to support them.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Issue Volume: Agents created 3% of Linear’s work a year ago; now it is more than half.
  • Pricing Model: Until June, Linear operated on entirely seat-based pricing.
  • Sales Strategy: Linear has never hired a single SDR. Companies are signing one-year deals and paid pilots rather than three-year contracts.
  • Financials: Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention.
  • Valuation: In August, employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation.

💡 Why It Matters

Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Most frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Companies have carved out budgets for AI tools that did not exist before, allowing products that fit within these budgets to skip the usual fight for spend. Cristina notes that Linear is lucky it is small enough to cannibalize itself, allowing the shift to agent-driven workflows without the drag of legacy enterprise commitments.

#Linear #AIAgents #DevTools #MCP #SaaS

Source: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO — Latent Space

item.title: Microsoft publishes open-source Model Context Protocol curriculum and Qdrant memory server

Microsoft publishes open-source Model Context Protocol curriculum and Qdrant memory server

Microsoft has released an open-source curriculum for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) alongside an official MCP server for Qdrant, enabling developers to build modular, secure AI workflows and implement semantic memory layers using specific language examples and vector search integration.

🧩 The MCP Curriculum

🧠 The Qdrant MCP Server

The release includes an official Model Context Protocol server for keeping and retrieving memories in the Qdrant vector search engine. This server acts as a semantic memory layer on top of the Qdrant database and is based on FastMCP.

Core Tools

  • qdrant-store: Stores information in the Qdrant database.
  • qdrant-find: Retrieves relevant information from the Qdrant database.

Configuration Details

Configuration is handled via environment variables, and the only command-line argument is --transport, which selects the transport protocol. You cannot provide both QDRANT_URL and QDRANT_LOCAL_PATH simultaneously.

Environment Variable Description
QDRANT_LOCAL_PATH Path to the local Qdrant database (alternative to QDRANT_URL)
EMBEDDING_PROVIDER Embedding provider to use (currently only “fastembed” is supported)
EMBEDDING_MODEL Name of the embedding model to use
QDRANT_SEARCH_LIMIT Maximum number of results to return from search

FASTMCP_PORT Port to run the server on (SSE and HTTP transports)

Before version 0.9.0, settings used the FASTMCP_SERVER_ prefix (e.g., FASTMCP_SERVER_HOST). The old names FASTMCP_SERVER_HOST, FASTMCP_SERVER_PORT, and FASTMCP_SERVER_DEBUG still work but are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. If both old and new names are set, the new name takes precedence.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway Networking Requirements for Private MCP and REST APIs
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway Networking Requirements for Private MCP and REST APIs

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway now supports agents that call internal REST APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, provided they meet specific network ownership and traffic inspection requirements.

🔍 Overview

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The Gateway connects to private targets through an Amazon VPC Lattice resource gateway. This update clarifies where to place the resource gateway, who owns each network component, and the configuration decisions required for traffic to cross a central firewall in both directions.

🧩 How it works

The AgentCore Gateway reaches private targets through two private endpoint modes:

  • Managed mode: AgentCore creates the resource gateway for you. This fits environments where the Gateway account can own the subnets it runs in.
  • Self-managed mode: You create the resource gateway and give the target a resource configuration. As documented, this places it in subnets with direct access to the backend, fitting environments that do not require inspection between the Gateway and the tool.

In the pattern built and tested in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (us-east-1), the network account owns the resource gateway and places it in subnets routed through AWS Transit Gateway. This ensures every request and reply between VPCs crosses the central firewall in an inspection VPC. The network team keeps ownership of every subnet, and traffic between the Gateway and private APIs and MCP servers crosses the central firewall in both directions.

⚙️ Key details

The architecture relies on specific VPC Lattice objects and sharing mechanisms:

  • Resource gateway: The Amazon VPC Lattice entry point into a VPC, utilizing elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in subnets you choose.
  • Resource configuration: A VPC Lattice object that names one backend (an internal load balancer or VPC endpoint DNS name and port) behind a resource gateway. This can be shared with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).

Key ownership and traffic rules include:

  • A network account owns every VPC, subnet, and AWS Transit Gateway attachment, sharing application subnets through AWS RAM.
  • The Gateway account can own subnets that reach your tools.
  • The Gateway and application accounts build only in subnets shared to them through AWS RAM.
  • Tools are reachable on public endpoints if central inspection is not required for that specific flow, but in the documented pattern, every flow between VPCs crosses the central firewall.
  • The central firewall in the inspection VPC inspects the traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers.

🚀 Availability

The pattern was validated in a lab with three member accounts and a management account in AWS Organizations. The AWS CloudFormation templates, test scripts, test evidence, and reference material (address plan, full validation checks, troubleshooting, quotas) are available in the companion repository.

item.title: Databricks introduces Skills for Genie One
item.description:
Databricks introduces Skills for Genie One

Databricks has introduced a new feature for Genie One called Skills, which adds a layer of control by defining specific workflow recipes that the agent can follow on demand to ensure consistent formats and outputs.

🧩 How it works

A skill is a durable, reusable asset that serves as a written record of how a team works, using plain language and the open Agent Skills format. Genie One leverages skills either when called directly by the user or when it decides a skill is relevant to the request.

  • Scope and Isolation: Guidance stays with the specific task rather than spilling into other work. Because Genie One only reads the skills it needs, keeping them specific and focused is advantageous for testing, fixing, and reusing them.
  • Chainable Assets: Small skills can be chained together; for example, updating a style guidelines skill once allows every other skill that uses it to pick up the change.
  • Judgment vs. Routines: While dashboards do the same thing every time, skills allow Genie One to make decisions, such as choosing the most important changes for leadership or following unusual results until they make sense.
  • Strict Rules: Skills define what must always appear, what to do when something is missing, and thresholds that decide what gets a closer look. For instance, a trading brief might always include a watch list even if nothing breached a threshold.

⚙️ Key details

Skills distinguish themselves from Genie Agents and Genie Ontology by focusing on the method rather than domain knowledge:

Component Function
Genie Ontology Tells Genie One what things mean.
Genie Agent Domain expert for one area (e.g., sales, finance, HR); knows metric definitions, tables, joins, and business rules.
Skill Recipe for a specific task: the steps, checklist, and output format.

For example, a sales pipeline Genie Agent knows the pipeline tables and stage definitions, while a “weekly forecast risk memo” skill instructs Genie One to compare current and previous pipeline data, flag slipped deals, and produce a one-page memo. The Genie Agent supplies domain knowledge, and the skill supplies the workflow.

💡 Why it matters

You can build a skill directly in Genie One by explaining your workflow in detail once, prompting the agent to interview you before writing the skill. Genie One draws on existing knowledge through Genie Ontology to focus questions on how you work rather than what your data means. Answering in plain language is enough for Genie One to write the skill. Once built, a skill can be published through Unity Gateway and used by any agent that supports MCP, including coding agents teams already use.

Consider using a skill when you find yourself explaining the same thing to Genie One more than once.

item.title: Rust SDK Adds Stable 2026-07-28 MCP Version with New Features
item.description:
Rust SDK Adds Stable 2026-07-28 MCP Version with New Features

This release brings the stable MCP 2026‑07‑28 specification to the Rust SDK, while remaining fully compatible with the 2025‑11‑25 release and earlier versions.

🔍 Overview

  • The SDK implements the stable MCP 2026-07-28 specification.
  • It remains fully compatible with the 2025-11-25 release and previous versions.

🧩 Features

  • Server discovery & negotiation
  • Transport‑neutral subscriptions
  • Long‑running tasks
  • Response caching
  • Multi‑round‑trip requests
  • Standard HTTP routing headers

⚙️ SDK Structure

  • Repository crates:
    • rmcp: core crate providing the RMCP protocol implementation
    • rmcp‑macros: procedural macro crate for generating RMCP tool implementations
  • Basic dependencies:
    • tokio
    • serde
  • JSON Schema generation (version 2020‑12):
    • schemars

📦 Installation & Setup

  • Add the latest published version: 
    1

    cargo add rmcp --features server
  • Or use the dev channel: 
    1

    cargo add rmcp --features server --git https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk --branch main

🚀 Server and Client Lifecycle

  • serve() uses the legacy MCP lifecycle:
    • The client sends initialize.
    • The server returns negotiated server information.
    • The client sends notifications/initialized.
  • Use ClientServiceExt::serve_with_lifecycle to select another lifecycle explicitly.
  • ClientLifecycleMode::Initialize is equivalent to the existing serve() behavior.
  • Discover startup does not send notifications/initialized; discovery completes startup.
  • Each subsequent request carries its protocol version, client information, and capabilities in _meta.
  • For a server, serve() waits for peer input that establishes the protocol lifecycle, such as initialize from a legacy client.
  • A stdio MCP server is normally launched by an MCP client as a child process.
  • Running the executable alone in a terminal can leave this await pending because no client has sent protocol messages yet.
  • After serve() returns, the service handles messages in the background.
  • You can run other asynchronous work, then use waiting() to wait for shutdown.
  • To cancel during startup, use serve_with_ct().

🛠️ Building a Service

  • Use ServerHandler or ClientHandler to build a service.
  • Await protocol startup, then receive a handle to the running service.

item.title: Event‑Driven Sync of MCP Server Tools to AWS Agent Registry
item.description:
Event‑Driven Sync of MCP Server Tools to AWS Agent Registry

When a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record is automatically refreshed via an event‑driven workflow.

🔍 Overview

  • An MCP server published in the AWS Agent Registry must keep its tool or schema record up‑to‑date.
  • An event‑driven workflow uses AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda to automate the update.
  • The solution works in both single‑account and multi‑account environments.

🏗️ Architecture

  • AWS CloudTrail – captures UpdateAgentRuntime API calls as management events.
  • Amazon EventBridge – routes matching events to a Lambda function; supports cross‑account forwarding.
  • AWS Lambda (sync function) – queries the MCP server, diffs the tool list against the registry, and updates the record when needed.
  • AWS Agent Registry – stores MCP server records and their tool schemas as the source of truth.
  • AgentCore Identity – brokers OAuth token exchanges so the Lambda can authenticate without storing secrets.
  • Account roles
    • Account A (registry account) owns the Agent Registry, EventBridge rule, sync Lambda, and CloudTrail logs.
    • Account B (MCP server account) hosts the MCP server runtime and the Amazon Cognito OAuth provider.

⚙️ How It Works

  1. A developer updates an MCP server in Account B; the server calls the UpdateAgentRuntime API (via AgentCore CLI or directly).
  2. CloudTrail in Account B records the call as a management event (≈ 5–15 min delay).
  3. EventBridge in Account B captures the CloudTrail event and forwards it to the default EventBridge bus in Account A (cross‑account rule when applicable).
  4. The EventBridge rule in Account A triggers the sync Lambda, passing the full CloudTrail event JSON.
  5. The Lambda extracts the runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) from the event and builds the MCP server’s invocation URL.
  6. The Lambda obtains a secure OAuth bearer token through AgentCore Identity.
  7. The Lambda calls the MCP server (initialize, then tools/list) to retrieve the latest tools information.
  8. The Lambda locates the corresponding registry record by ARN, compares the retrieved schema with the stored one, and updates the record if a change is detected.
  9. The process assumes the registry already contains a pre‑registered record for the MCP server; the Lambda updates existing records only and does not create new ones.

🚀 Availability

  • The same workflow runs unchanged in a single‑account deployment where the registry, Lambda, EventBridge rule, and MCP server all reside in Account A.
  • In a multi‑account deployment, runtime events flow securely from Account B to Account A before the Lambda performs the sync.

item.title: Adding PKI‑Based Authentication to the Model Context Protocol with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS
item.description:
Adding PKI‑Based Authentication to the Model Context Protocol with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS

Multi‑agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations, but MCP has no built-in authentication standard. This post shows how to fill that gap using Keyfactor EJBCA together with AWS services.

🔍 Overview

  • Multi‑agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources.
  • MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations.
  • MCP has no built‑in authentication standard.

🛠️ Architecture

The solution combines Keyfactor EJBCA with several AWS managed services and implements three authentication layers that protect each trust boundary in the agent communication chain.

AWS Service Role in the architecture
Amazon Bedrock (via Strands Agents SDK) LLM inference for agents
Amazon RDS for MySQL Application database accessed through MCP tools
Amazon Simple Email Service (SES) Email delivery for the Email Agent
AWS Secrets Manager Secure storage for PKCS12 bundles, tokens, and metadata
Amazon EC2 Hosts Keycloak identity provider and EJBCA PKI server

🔐 Authentication Layers

  1. Layer 1 – User Auth (User → System)
    • Uses OAuth together with an X.509 certificate and delegation minting.
    • Provides user identity and credential binding.
  2. Layer 2 – Agent‑to‑Agent (Agent → Agent)
    • Relies on signed request envelopes containing proof‑of‑possession, a nonce, and a timestamp.
    • Guarantees caller identity, request freshness, and prevents replay.
  3. Layer 3 – MCP Auth (Agent → Tool Server)
    • Combines a scoped token, the signed envelope, and a delegation assertion.
    • Covers all identities, creates a full authorization chain, and incorporates OCSP validation.

⚙️ Key Components & Controls

  • Signed request envelopes – give cryptographic proof‑of‑possession on every agent call.
  • User‑signed delegation assertions – authorize agents without sharing credentials.
  • RFC 8693 audience‑scoped tokens – limit exposure if a token is disclosed.
  • Real‑time OCSP revocation checking – propagates credential changes instantly across agents.
  • EJBCA Enterprise – a PKI platform that supports high‑availability deployment, REST API automation, X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management via web console and REST API.
  • Keyfactor – a machine‑identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide.

🚀 Deployment Options

  • EJBCA can be deployed on‑premises, in containers, or on Amazon EC2.
  • Designed for high‑availability and REST API automation to integrate with AWS services.

💡 Why it matters

  • The added layers supply authentication and authorization that MCP originally lacked.
  • Cryptographic proof‑of‑possession, delegations, scoped tokens, and immediate revocation together reduce the risk of credential misuse while preserving the flexibility of multi‑agent AI workflows.

AWS Agent Registry enables runtime tool discovery for enterprise AI agents

AWS Agent Registry is a managed service designed for cataloging and discovering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agents, and agent skills to address the limitations of hardcoded tool integration in enterprise systems.

💡 Why it matters

In enterprise SaaS engagements, systems often expose hundreds of internal APIs for customer data, inventory, orders, support, and pricing. Relying on build-time wiring for these tools can create several bottlenecks:

  • Scalability: Hardcoded tools function well for a few, degrade at a few dozen, and become unmanageable beyond that.
  • Performance: Models may spend more tokens disambiguating tool names than reasoning about user requests.
  • Operational Overhead: Each new capability typically requires a code change in the orchestrator, a redeploy, and coordinated releases across teams.

🧩 How it works

Instead of compiling every tool into the agent, an orchestrator can discover relevant tools at runtime:

  1. Registration: Publishers register searchable descriptions and protocol-specific descriptors.
  2. Search: The orchestrator sends a natural-language query to the AWS Agent Registry data plane.
  3. Response: The registry returns record identity, name, description, record type, status, version, and protocol descriptors (such as an A2A agent card or MCP server metadata).
  4. Client Construction: The orchestrator constructs a client for each returned record based on the descriptor type.
  5. Execution: An ephemeral inner agent is built using only the dynamically discovered tools. The LLM selects the appropriate tool, synthesizes the result for the user, and the inner agent and clients are torn down after the turn.

⚙️ Key details

To maintain security, registry search results do not return authentication schemes or invocation credentials. The application must apply credentials through a separate, trusted configuration path.

item.title: Amazon Quick resource migration automated with Bedrock AgentCore MCP server
item.description:
Amazon Quick resource migration automated with Bedrock AgentCore MCP server

Amazon Quick is Amazon’s agentic AI companion built for work. Moving its resources – chat agents, action connectors, knowledge bases, flows, and spaces – from a development AWS account to a production account has traditionally been a manual, error‑prone chore.

🔍 Overview

  • Enterprises often run separate AWS accounts for development, QA, and production.
  • There is no native one‑click way to promote validated Quick resources into the next account; teams must rebuild each resource by hand.
  • The Quick Resource Migrator is a sample Model Context Protocol (MCP) server hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this cross‑account promotion with a single tool call.

🛠️ How it works

  • The migrator composes the Create, Read, Update, and List API calls of the Amazon Quick API into a repeatable workflow; it never issues a delete, so a run only adds or updates.
  • It is resource‑driven – you pick a resource type (agent, connector, knowledge base, flow, or space) and select resources by ID, name, or all.
  • The server runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime and can be triggered from Amazon Quick or any MCP‑compatible client.
Resource Type Migration actions
Chat agents Recreate with custom instructions, identity, tone, starter prompts, welcome message; re‑attach action connectors (remapped to target).
Action connectors Recreate configuration; secret values never read – placeholders are created then re‑authenticated in target.
Knowledge bases Register in target, recreate data source, copy permissions; for S3‑backed bases also provision target bucket and bucket policy (documents are not copied).
Flows Recreate from definition; matched by name – same‑named flow is updated, otherwise a new flow is created.
Spaces Recreate in target and re‑link to agents, connectors, and knowledge bases with ARN remapping; agents are automatically re‑linked when a space migrates.

⚙️ Key features

  • Idempotent – safe to re‑run; performs upserts (creates missing resources, updates existing ones).
  • Permission fidelity – calls Describe*Permissions on the source and replays identical actions in the target, remapping ARNs.
  • Versioned backup – every update is preceded by a backup written to Amazon S3, giving a full history for review or rollback.
  • Read‑only preview – reports exactly what would be created or updated before committing.
  • Single‑call promotion – a chosen set of resources is promoted in one operation.
  • Programmable – all resources are managed through the Amazon Quick API (full CRUDL lifecycle).
  • Open source – full source code is available in the aws-samples repository.

🚀 Availability

  • The MCP server is hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime.
  • It can be invoked from Amazon Quick or any client that supports MCP.
  • Source code and deployment instructions are published in the public aws-samples GitHub repository.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enterprises with separate development and production AWS accounts can eliminate a manual, error‑prone promotion process.
  • Consistent permission copying and versioned backups reduce risk of misconfiguration in production.
  • Idempotent upserts and preview mode enable safe, repeatable migrations, supporting CI/CD pipelines and governance.
  • By automating promotion, teams can focus on building and evaluating agentic AI solutions rather than on repetitive infrastructure work.

item.title: ProvenanceGuard Introduces Post-Generation Verification for MCP Agents
item.description:
ProvenanceGuard Introduces Post-Generation Verification for MCP Agents

ProvenanceGuard has been developed as a post-generation verification layer that operates on top of black-box MCP agents to verify the accuracy of agent-produced answers.

🧩 How it works

The system runs after an agent produces an answer and reads the captured MCP trace, including tool outputs and source IDs, without requiring the agent to be retrained. The verification process follows these steps:

  • Claim Decomposition: A local language model breaks the answer into specific claims.
  • Source Identification: MiniLM is used to find the source most relevant to each claim.
  • Support Verification: A DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks if the source actually supports the claim.
  • Comparison: The system compares the identified source with the one the answer names or implies.
  • Verdict: It emits a per-claim source verdict and a global answer-level allow or block decision.

⚙️ Key details

  • Literal Value Checking: The verifier closely checks numbers, dates, or identifiers; if they are absent from the source, they cannot pass based on plausibility alone.
  • Repair Mechanism: Blocked answers can undergo a RARR-style repair step for a source-grounded revision or safe fallback, which is then re-verified.
  • Transparency: Unlike other checkers, ProvenanceGuard records the connection between each claim and its supporting tool output for reviewer oversight.

📊 Performance and Testing

ProvenanceGuard was tested using 281 real traces from a medical agent utilizing research articles and patient records. In a main test where human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers:

  • It caught 138 of 139 claims that experts said should not pass.
  • It let one claim through.
  • It flagged 67 claims for review or repair that experts considered supported.
  • It identified the correct source for claims with an identifiable source approximately 86% of the time.

When compared to other support checkers, ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the measure of catching claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks:

item.title: Implementing Multi-Gate Authorization for MCP Tools on Amazon Quick
item.description:
Implementing Multi-Gate Authorization for MCP Tools on Amazon Quick

Amazon Quick now supports a multi-gate authorization pattern for Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool invocations, utilizing an interceptor to evaluate OpenID Connect (OIDC) JSON Web Token (JWT) claims in sequence.

🔍 Overview

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that connects applications to internal tools, databases, and APIs to reduce the need for custom integrations. In this implementation, Amazon Quick connects to an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway—a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore—which provides the JWT validation layer and HTTP endpoint between clients and MCP tools.

🧩 How it works

Authorization is managed through a single AWS Lambda REQUEST interceptor attached to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. This interceptor processes JWT claims through four independent gates in a fixed sequence:

Gate Name Enforcement/Claim Purpose Requirement
1 MFA verification IdP / Conditional Access Policy Require MFA before token issuance Conditional
2 Country geo-fence ctry Restrict access to approved countries Conditional (REQUIRE_COUNTRY=true)
3 Group RBAC groups Map group membership to reader, author, or admin policies Always (core gate)
4 Tool permission Policy allowlists Verify the requested tool exists in the matched policy Always (core gate)

⚙️ Key details

  • Identity Provider: Microsoft Entra ID serves as the IdP. It enforces the Conditional Access Policy for MFA before issuing a token.
  • Configuration: Gates are configured via environment variables. While Gates 3 and 4 are always active, Gates 1 and 2 can be disabled by omitting the environment variables or setting them to false.
  • MFA Validation: Setting REQUIRE_MFA enables an additional check of the amr claim inside the interceptor for IdPs that record MFA evidence in the token.
  • Access Control: Role-based permissions establish a read/write boundary where readers can query risks but cannot create, update, or delete them, while administrators can bypass conditional gates.
  • Compliance: Every mutation must produce an immutable audit record for forensic and compliance requirements.

This pattern is demonstrated using a fictional example involving AnyCompany Global Services, which uses MCP tools on Amazon Quick to access a multi-tenant risk register hosted on Amazon DynamoDB.

item.title: The nine parts of every AI agent
item.description:
The nine parts of every AI agent

Every AI agent, from vendor demos to internal prototypes, is built from the same nine components. These parts define how agents operate, interact, and deliver results in commercial environments.

🧩 The nine parts

  • Memory: Everything the agent knows about you and your work that wasn’t in the message you just sent it. For commercial work, this includes project records like subcontract packages, marked-up drawings, diary entries, labour returns, early warnings, and correspondence.
  • Context engineering: Choosing the relevant slice of memory for the task at hand. Giving the AI everything produces a worse answer, more slowly, at higher cost.
  • Skills: A complete piece of work the agent knows how to do end to end, in the right order, with judgement calls marked. Writing one out properly takes about an hour and provides inputs, steps, judgement calls, and what a good output looks like.
  • Tools: How the agent reaches the outside world. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard that lets a model connect to a live system and read from it directly.
  • Systems: A commercial agent needs five systems, four vendors, and often a shared drive with folders named “FINAL v3 USE THIS ONE”.
  • Data extraction: For each record, name the system it lives in, then ask whether data comes out of it any way other than someone exporting to Excel on a Friday. Where the answer is no, that is the bottleneck.
  • Runtime: The loop where the agent plans, acts, looks at what came back, adjusts, retries when something fails, and keeps going until the job is done. Assessing an event isn’t one question, it’s fifteen in sequence, with answers changing subsequent questions.
  • Triggers: What start the work without anyone asking. The most obviously valuable part, because most commercial issues arise from someone not looking on the right day.

⚙️ Key details

  • Memory already exists somewhere, either as a diary submitted through a system or a scanned signed sheet in a folder. Getting it across that line costs money.
  • A short list of relevant context is a rule you can hand over, and it’s the difference between an agent that answers in seconds for pennies and one that takes a minute and costs more to be less accurate.
  • Products with a real runtime have a clear answer. Products without one change the subject to the quality of their model.
  • In every case, somebody knew the rule for triggers.

#AIagents #memory #contextengineering #runtime #MCP #commercialAI

item.title: Harness engineering emerges as key to AI agent performance
item.description:
Harness engineering emerges as key to AI agent performance

A new discipline called harness engineering is shaping how language models are turned into functional agents. Early 2026 leaderboards show that the harness—software scaffolding around a model—can influence performance as much as the model itself.

🔍 Overview

Harness engineering is the discipline of designing the software that surrounds a language model and turns it into a working agent. It covers context delivery, tool interfaces, memory, and sandboxes. The model supplies the reasoning, while the harness decides what the model sees, what it can do, what it remembers, and where it runs.

⚙️ Key details

  • An agent harness is the software scaffolding around a model.
  • Anthropic describes it as ’the loop, tools, context management, and guardrails that turn raw intelligence into a working agent'.
  • METR called it scaffolding back in 2023: scaffolding plus a model equals an agent.

Performance impact

  • On early 2026 leaderboards, the harness moved the score at least as much as the model did.
  • On the Terminal-Bench 2.0 leaderboard, Claude Opus 4.6 scored between 58.0% and 74.7% across seven harnesses, all submitted between 5 and 23 February 2026.
    • The highest of the seven was Terminus-KIRA from KRAFTON AI at 74.7%.
    • Confidence intervals sit near plus or minus 2.5 to 2.9 points, so a 16.7 point spread is not noise.
  • On SWE-bench Verified’s bash-only board, nine frontier models ran the identical mini-swe-agent scaffold at matched reasoning effort, all submitted on 17 February 2026. Their scores spanned just 66.6% to 76.8%, a 10.2 point gap.
  • On the newer Terminal-Bench 2.1 board, harness spreads collapse to between 0.2 and 8.1 points once reasoning effort and submission dates are matched, so the gap appears to be narrowing.

Components

  • Tool interfaces: Tool dispatch turns a model’s request into a real action. The model returns a tool-use block, the harness runs it and returns the result, and the loop repeats until the model stops asking.

    • The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how an agent reaches those tools, and calls itself ‘an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems’.
    • Anthropic created MCP and donated it to the Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025.
    • The MCP specification warns that tools ‘represent arbitrary code execution’.

  • Memory: State persistence is how an agent survives its own context window.

    • Context compaction is the usual answer, and the Claude Agent SDK summarizes earlier messages as the limit approaches.
    • Compaction is lossy, and Anthropic says so: ‘While compaction preserves continuity, it doesn’t give the agent a clean slate.’
    • Durable state therefore belongs outside the transcript: Claude Code re-injects project memory files after compaction, and LangGraph gives agents short-term memory through checkpointers and long-term memory through stores.

  • Sandboxes: A sandbox is the boundary between a mistake and an incident.

    • Claude Code’s built-in sandbox uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap plus socat on Linux and WSL2, and by default a command writes only to the working directory and the session temp directory.
    • OpenAI Codex offers read-only, workspace-write and danger-full-access modes, runs with network off by default, and applies one rule: ‘deny always wins over allow.’
    • Heavier isolation goes as far as microVMs such as Firecracker, and E2B says its same-region sandboxes ‘start in less than 200 ms’.

  • Guardrails: Guardrails decide what an agent may attempt, and isolation decides what the attempt can reach.

    • Anthropic draws the line cleanly: ‘Permission modes decide whether a tool call runs and whether you are prompted first. Isolation restricts what a command can access once it runs.’
    • Claude Code ranks its permission modes from Manual up to bypassPermissions, with acceptEdits, plan, auto and dontAsk in between, and deny rules block in every one of them.
    • The OpenAI Agents SDK adds input, output and tool guardrails, any of which can raise a tripwire and halt the run.

💡 Why it matters

  • The core difference is scope: prompt engineering shapes one exchange with a model, while harness engineering shapes the system around the model for the length of a task.
  • Neither replaces the other: a harness contains prompts, and a bad system prompt sinks a good agent.
  • Coding agents are where harness engineering stopped being optional.
  • OpenAI’s account of adopting Codex is blunt about why: ‘Early progress was slower than we expected, not because Codex was incapable, but because the environment was underspecified.’

🧩 How it works

  • Anthropic defines context engineering as ’the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference'.

#AIagents #harnessengineering #LLMs #agenticAI #MCP #sandboxing

Source: What is Harness Engineering? The AI Agent Scaffolding Guide

item.title: OpenClaw 2.0 Introduces Faster Startup and Strict Security Boundaries
item.description:
OpenClaw 2.0 Introduces Faster Startup and Strict Security Boundaries

OpenClaw 2.0 has arrived, bringing a 575 ms Control UI startup time and a new One Trust Boundary Per Gateway architecture to address security and performance in agentic frameworks.

🔍 Overview

The agentic framework landscape has shifted with OpenClaw 2.0, which introduces significant performance and security improvements. The standout feature is the reduced Control UI startup time, now at 575 ms, a drastic improvement from the previous iteration. This optimization makes agent environments feel instantaneous, eliminating the sluggishness often experienced during rapid prototyping.

⚙️ Key details

  • Sub-600ms UI Startup: Achieved through aggressive tree-shaking and pre-compiled model-context bundles.
  • One Trust Boundary Per Gateway: A mandatory hardware-backed security protocol that isolates the execution environment of each individual agent gateway.
  • Native MCP Support: Seamless integration with the Model Context Protocol, enabling direct communication with models like Gemini 3.1 and Mistral Large 3.
  • Asynchronous State Persistence: Uses Mem0 for faster memory retrieval, reducing latency in long-running sessions.
  • Unified Gateway API: A standard interface for both local and cloud-hosted environments.
  • Auto-Reconciliation Engine: Automatically detects and resets agent context when it drifts from its system prompt.
  • Plugin Sandboxing: All third-party plugins run in isolated containers, preventing host environment access.
  • Enhanced Telemetry: Real-time logging of token usage and latency spikes per gateway.
  • Dynamic Context Pruning: Smarter token management prioritizing relevant state data over stale chat history.
  • Websocket Optimization: Reduced handshake overhead for real-time agent-to-agent communication.
  • Type-Safe Agent Definitions: Built-in TypeScript support for strict interface definitions.
  • Custom Error Handling: Granular control over agent recovery from failed model inference.
  • Multi-Region Support: Optimized routing for agents deployed across global cloud clusters.
  • Versioning Middleware: Ability to run multiple versions of agent logic simultaneously for A/B testing.
  • Built-in RAG Connectors: Native support for Qdrant and Pinecone for faster data ingestion.

🧩 How it works

OpenClaw 2.0 enforces a strict One Trust Boundary Per Gateway architecture, isolating each agent’s execution environment. This prevents cross-agent contamination and prompt injection attacks, which were common in late 2025. The framework now requires explicit definitions for where data crosses boundaries, adopting a zero-trust model by default. This is a departure from the more fluid, interconnected architectures of frameworks like CrewAI or LangGraph.

💡 Why it matters

  • Every millisecond of initialization is billed as compute time, making speed improvements critical for high-frequency tasks like automated trading or rapid-fire data analysis.
  • The new security model addresses ‘agent poisoning’ attacks, where malicious prompts compromise entire orchestration layers.
  • Enterprise teams in regulated industries like finance and healthcare can now adopt OpenClaw 2.0 due to its security hardening.
  • Developers using OpenClaw 1.x may face migration friction, as the new security requirements demand significant refactoring of existing gateways.
  • The framework is becoming more opinionated, which may alienate users preferring the flexibility of AutoGen or the simplicity of Swarm.

🚀 Availability

OpenClaw 2.0 is now available, positioning itself as a secure foundation for the next generation of AI agents. The developer community has reacted positively, particularly to the speed improvements and security enhancements, though some note the added complexity in setup.
